conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Emily, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and understand how things have felt for you lately. I’ll be guiding us through a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us pick up on signs of depression, anxiety, and self-harm that can sometimes show up after a baby arrives. Nothing you say today will leave this room unless you or your baby’s safety is at immediate risk, so please feel free to speak openly. We’ll move through one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no right or wrong replies. Ready to begin?

First, thinking back over the past seven days: have you still been able to look forward to things you normally enjoy, or has that sense of pleasure slipped away?

It’s… mostly gone. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a show I liked—but now, even when I try, it just feels flat. Once in a while I’ll still smile if the baby does something cute, but it’s like the color’s been drained out of everything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Honestly… not really. I might give a little laugh if my partner says something, but it feels forced, and it’s gone in a second. Nothing feels genuinely funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I’ll tell myself “I used to love this,” but when the moment comes—like meeting a friend or even taking a walk—it just feels like going through the motions. Sometimes I still hope I’ll enjoy it, but the feeling barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding him right or I missed some cue. Even when my partner says he’s just being a baby, I still feel it’s my fault. I keep replaying little mistakes and thinking a “better mom” wouldn’t make them.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, a lot of the time. I’ll be sitting there with the baby sleeping soundly, and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure something bad is about to happen—like he’ll stop breathing or I’ll drop him. I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t switch the thoughts off. Some nights I just stare at the monitor waiting for something to go wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it hits me out of nowhere—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and suddenly I’m convinced something awful is about to happen. There doesn’t have to be a trigger; it just sweeps over me like a wave. I’ll check that the baby’s okay, then check again, but the feeling lingers.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. Even little stuff—laundry, answering a text—seems huge. I’ll start one chore, the baby cries, and suddenly I’m crying too because I can’t keep up. I get through it, but it’s like I’m always one step from dropping everything.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s been hard. I lie down exhausted, but my mind just keeps spinning—thinking I didn’t do enough today, worrying about tomorrow, picturing worst-case scenarios. Most nights it takes me over an hour to fall asleep, and when the baby wakes I can’t drift off again because the anxious thoughts start right back up.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start rolling down my face—I couldn’t even tell you exactly why. Some afternoons I end up sitting on the nursery floor feeling hollow and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it’s happened maybe twice this week. The other night I was folding onesies and just started sobbing—no real reason, just this wave of sadness. I try to keep it quiet so my partner won’t worry, but the tears come before I can stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s popped into my head a couple times. Nothing planned—I’d never leave my baby—but when everything feels crushing, I’ll get this quick image of just not wanting to be here anymore. It scares me, and I shove it away, but the fact that it shows up at all terrifies me.

You've shared that the joy you once found in everyday moments has faded, replaced by a daily heaviness and frequent tears. Even when your baby delights you, the color feels drained from life, and simple tasks loom like mountains. Unwanted worries about your son's safety race through your mind, especially at night, making it hard to fall or return to sleep. You often blame yourself for normal infant fussiness, replaying small mistakes while feeling you should be a "better mom," and occasional brief thoughts of not wanting to be here frighten you. Your honesty about these feelings shows real courage, and many new mothers in similar circumstances have found relief once they received the right support.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Response indicates inability to experience genuine enjoyment or humor, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes almost no enjoyment and "going through the motions," aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame, attributing baby's fussiness to her own perceived mistakes and replaying errors despite reassurance, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intrusive, uncontrolled worries occurring "a lot of the time" with physical anxiety symptoms, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes being overwhelmed "most days," feeling unable to manage routine tasks, and frequent tearfulness—clearly matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep driven by persistent anxious/unhappy thoughts, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily sadness, unexplained crying, and persistent low mood—closest to "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying twice in the past week with unexpected, overwhelming sadness—fits "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive self-harm thoughts "a couple times" that are distressing but not acted upon, aligning with "Sometimes".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27 on the <med>Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale</med> falls well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depression with peripartum onset. The pattern of <sym>anhedonia</sym>, pervasive <sym>sadness</sym>, excessive self-blame, recurrent panic-type episodes, sleep disruption, and passive suicidal thoughts meets core <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for <med>Major Depressive Disorder</med>; the onset within one year postpartum supports the peripartum specifier. Item 10 ≥1 also flags immediate safety risk. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Share these screening results with your OB/midwife so they can expedite referral and coordinate care
3. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you until professional help is in place; avoid being alone with the baby if thoughts intensify
4. Call 988 (U.S.) or your local crisis line if urges to self-harm become stronger or you feel unsafe
5. Begin gentle daily routine: one short outdoor walk, balanced meals, and brief rest when baby sleeps; small achievable goals reduce overwhelm
6. Consider peer support (Postpartum Support International warmline 1-800-944-4773) for 24/7 text/chat with moms who've recovered
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS within one week to monitor symptom change after starting safety plan or treatment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant ≤ 1 yr)

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Daily low mood, frequent crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to rumination (Q7)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re parenting (Q3)  
- Recurrent, intrusive anxious worries about infant safety; panic-type episodes without clear trigger (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks (Q6)

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days,” cause subjective distress and functional impairment.

Risk flags:
- Passive self-harm ideation (“quick image of not wanting to be here”) without intent or plan; patient reports fear of these thoughts (Q10)

Screening impression:  
High clinical concern for major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; safety risk requires immediate follow-up assessment.

Next step: Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive evaluation and safety planning.
